title: Working in Your Own Language — Module Quiz

items.q: Models answer better in English mainly because:
options: English grammar is simpler to model
Far more English text was available to train on
They are developed in English-speaking countries
items.explain: More text means more phrasing, more subject matter, and more of the world discussed through that language.

items.q: Speaker count and resource level are:
options: Closely correlated
Only loosely related — languages with tens of millions of speakers can be low-resource
Inversely related
items.explain: The languages served worst are not the smallest ones, which is the injustice worth naming.

items.q: Which symptom of a lower-resource language is most often missed?
options: Stiff, translated-sounding phrasing
A higher rate of factual errors about the world
Shorter answers
items.explain: Awkward phrasing is obvious; degraded facts about local law, history and institutions are not.

items.q: Published multilingual benchmarks are insufficient because:
options: They are usually out of date
They average across languages, tasks and subjects — yours is one of each
They only measure translation
items.explain: A model can be strong at conversational Hindi and weak at Hindi legal vocabulary. The average tells you neither.

items.q: In a personal language test, the most important and most skipped item is:
options: A factual question about your own region
A formal writing task
A constrained instruction
items.explain: Awkward phrasing is easy to spot; degraded regional facts are not.

items.q: Why test the same prompts on a second assistant?
options: To identify the generally best assistant
The gap between assistants is often larger than between languages, and varies by language
In case one becomes unavailable
items.explain: There is no general winner in your language — only a winner for your language and your tasks.

items.q: Back-translation must use a fresh conversation because:
options: It is faster
Otherwise the model has your original in context and reproduces it rather than re-translating
The context window would overflow
items.explain: In the same thread you get a comforting match that tested nothing.

items.q: Which error does back-translation reliably fail to catch?
options: A changed number
A politeness level that is grammatically perfect and insultingly informal
A dropped qualifier
items.explain: It checks meaning, not appropriateness. A rude translation back-translates perfectly.

items.q: Fluent modern translation is more dangerous than older clumsy translation because:
options: It is wrong more often
Clumsiness was a free warning signal, and fluency removed it
It is harder to reverse
items.explain: The error rate fell but did not vanish, while the signal telling you to be careful disappeared.

items.q: Mixing languages in a prompt usually causes problems with:
options: The model understanding you
The output language, which defaults to English when unspecified
Response length
items.explain: Models handle code-switched input well; the ambiguity is about what comes back.

items.q: The most effective instruction for professional writing in your language:
options: Ask for simpler vocabulary
List the terms that must stay in English
Request a longer answer
items.explain: A doctor writing in Bengali does not want 'hypertension' rendered into classical Bengali.

items.q: 'Reason in English, answer in my language' is the wrong approach when:
options: The task is analytical
Local context is the substance — local law, convention, what is normal where you are
The answer must be long
items.explain: You receive a translation of English-shaped reasoning, which may not know those things.

items.q: The assumption that breaks most name handling:
options: That names are short
One given name plus one family name, in Latin script
That names are unique
items.explain: Mononyms, patronymics, family-name-first ordering and multiple family names all fall outside it.

items.q: Why is inconsistent transliteration more than cosmetic?
options: It looks unprofessional
The same person becomes two records, and searching for them fails
It lengthens documents
items.explain: Names are identifiers, not just words.

items.q: In a form you build, names should be:
options: Split into first and last name fields
One field, full character range, editable later, never auto-corrected
Validated against a list of known names
items.explain: Ask separately for a sort key or greeting if you genuinely need one.

items.q: Register failure is more serious than phrasing failure because:
options: It is harder to correct
Awkward phrasing reads as effort; wrong register reads as disrespect
It affects more languages
items.explain: In many languages politeness is grammar, and native speakers hear the wrong choice immediately.

items.q: Rather than asking a model to 'be polite', you should:
options: Ask for formal language
State who you are, who they are, the relationship, and the form to use
Ask for a shorter message
items.explain: "Polite" means nothing across honorific systems; the relationship is the information that matters.

items.q: Back-translation cannot verify register because:
options: It only works between related languages
English flattens the distinction, so plain and honorific forms return the same English
Register is not part of meaning
items.explain: The check passes while the message is still wrong. Only a speaker can verify it.

items.q: The central trap in learning a language with an assistant:
options: It is too slow for real practice
You cannot evaluate its errors — if you could, you would not be learning
It refuses to use other languages
items.explain: Verification assumes you can verify. Here that assumption fails by construction.

items.q: Asking 'would a native speaker say this?' produces:
options: A reliable report from the speech community
A plausibility judgement that is frequently wrong
A refusal
items.explain: It knows what is grammatical far better than what is actually said.

items.q: Why is this especially suited to a half-known heritage language?
options: Heritage languages are usually high-resource
You already have the ear, so you can catch what a beginner cannot; only production is missing
Translation between related languages is more accurate
items.explain: Unlimited low-stakes practice supplies production, and your instinct is the check a beginner lacks.

items.q: Which task favours working in your own language?
options: Complex multi-step analysis
Anything involving local law, register, or a local reader
Generating a long list of options
items.explain: English tends to win where you judge quality yourself; your language wins where local context or register is the substance.

items.q: The best way to avoid doing the work twice:
options: Compose separately in both languages
Draft once in whichever language suits the task, then convert
Always draft in English first
items.explain: One piece of thinking, one conversion, one check — unless register carries the meaning.

items.q: A personal glossary is valuable because it:
options: Removes the need for back-translation
Fixes in one line most of what back-translation cannot catch
Speeds up generation
items.explain: Untranslated terms, agreed renderings, name spellings and register instructions are exactly the round trip's blind spots.
